content: js-build-tools Centralize the build process for Node.js, JS and TypeScript projects into a single tool suite. Goals Using this tool suite, you can: - Parse TypeScript into JS distribution files - Create formatted distribution files to be used in a node / commonjs environment. - Bundle your distribution files to be used in a browser environment. - Run tests and watch for changes. - Generate jsdoc readme files. - Generate real HTML documentation straight from your source - TypeDoc for a TypeScript project (a module for each of your folders), or jsdoc with a modern theme for a plain JavaScript one. - Copy files (a bundle, or anything else) to another location, on demand. Installation In your project's root directory, run: npm install --save-dev gulp js-build-tools (or yarn add --dev gulp js-build-tools if you use Yarn). It is recommended to install gulp with the -g flag, so that you can run it with gulp instead of node modules/.bin/gulp. Configuration In your project's root directory, create a build-tools.config.json file. This can contain any of the following (values provided are the defaults): Create your local gulpfile.js In your project's root directory, create a gulpfile.js file, in here you can require any of the functions you need. For example: Common JS ES Module Verify your tasks are available by running gulp --tasks. Configure Babel Depending on how you wrote your test files, Jest may require some Babel configuration. Create a babel.config.js file in the root directory of your project. You can then use the recommended configuration by requiring the babel.config.js file into your own configuration file. Example: Configure ES Modules (.mjs) It is not recommended to use "type": "module" in the package.json to enable ES Modules. This is because some dependencies still rely on common JS syntax (ex: babel, jest, jsdoc). So, to use ES Modules, you can use the .mjs extension on your files instead. There are different downsides to using the .mjs extension to consider. The jsdoc generation can only read .js files, and the provided test runner Jest will need to be configured. Update the test config as follows: There is an additional file you need to get Jest working, add a jest.config.js file. While we have already added these configurations above in the "options", there seems to be a bug where the "transform" does not work in that context. Add the following to your jest.config.js: Configure HTML JS Documentation, full manual control (optional, advanced) For most projects, docs.enabled with docs.method: 'jsdoc' (see 'Configure HTML documentation' below) is the simpler path - no .jsdoc.conf.js file to maintain by hand, wired straight into gulp build/gulp docs. This section is for when you want full, direct control over jsdoc's own config instead (a plugin or option this project's own generated config does not expose, for example). Create a .jsdoc.conf.js file and add the following: Configure what the browser bundle leaves out (optional) A dependency can be reached from your code without being needed in the browser, and bundling it can add a lot of size. Two settings in browser handle this, both take module names or file paths (see browserify's b.ignore(file) and b.exclude(file)): Configure additional browser bundles (optional) By default a project produces exactly one browser bundle, from dist.main/browser.name/browser.ignore/ browser.exclude above. browser.bundles adds more bundles alongside it - for example a render-only variant built from a different entry point than the full bundle. Each entry only needs to specify what's actually different about that bundle; anything left out falls back to the primary bundle's own value: For the gulpConfig module's own get/set functions (read or override a resolved configuration value from your own code, by the same dot-notation path a setting has in the JSON above), see the generated reference below. Configure including ESM files in the generated readme (optional) The readme generator (jsdoc-to-markdown) only recognizes .js files, even though it parses real ESM import/ export syntax just fine once it reads one - the file extension is the only thing it filters on, not the content. readme.fromEsm names .mjs files to document anyway: each one is read, rewritten (every top-level export const/ export function/export class becomes a plain declaration plus a trailing module.exports = { ... } - the same shape jsdoc-to-markdown already documents cleanly, since that rewrite is exactly what this project's own gulp.config.mjs needs it for) and written to a temp .js file outside your project entirely, which is cleaned up again once the readme generator has read it. Other export forms (export default, re-exports, export { a, b } lists) are left untouched in whatever way jsdoc-to-markdown already handles ESM - restructure a file to use named exports if you want it documented this cleanly: Configure copy files (optional) Copy files (a bundle, or anything else) to another location - any number of entries, each independent. Unlike every other task here, this is never run automatically as part of gulp build - what this copies is often the live, publicly-reachable version of something, so publishing it should be a deliberate step your own script opts into, not a side effect of a routine local build. Add the following to the exports in your build-tools.config.json: If you also export copyFiles from your gulpfile you can run it on its own with gulp copyFiles, and can then add your own script for it, for example "publish:bundle": "gulp copyFiles". Configure move fonts (optional) Be able to copy a source directory of fonts into the distribution path. Add the following to the exports in your build-tools.config.json: Configure move and minify images (optional) Be able to copy and reduce the file size of images into an output path. Add the following to the exports in your build-tools.config.json: Configure SASS (optional) SASS support is built-in, this enables conversion of SASS files to CSS for web projects. Add the following to the exports in your build-tools.config.json: Configure TypeScript (optional) Create a tsconfig.json file in your project root with the following: The pattern for "include" should match your .ts files (and leave out the tests, which can stay .test.js files). The actual pattern used to compile comes from build-tools.config.json as the 'typescript.from' setting. To create the ts declaration files, you must add the "declaration": true. The typescript package is an optional peer dependency, install it in your project with npm install --save-dev typescript (versions 5.0 up to, but not including, 7 are supported). When you write relative imports, leave the .js extension off (import a from './a'), because they stop resolving once the target is a .ts file. The compile only builds .ts files while typescript.enabled is on, so convert a whole library at once. Add the following to the exports in your build-tools.config.json: The js-to-markdown only works on .js files, so we run the readme search on the built dist files. Also, we want to register the tsconfig.json we created earlier and will alter the processes to build for TypeScript. Update babel.config.js with the following: Configure HTML documentation (optional) jsdoc-to-markdown (the readme generator) only reads .js files, so the types in your .ts files (and the comments on them) never reach the readme it generates, and even for a plain JavaScript project a single markdown readme is a thinner result than a real browsable site. Instead, docs.enabled generates real HTML documentation straight from your source, with either engine: - TypeDoc (for a TypeScript project) - every folder in your source directory becomes a module of the documentation, the default export of each file (one function per file) is listed under the name of the file, and everything else a file exports (for example the types in a types.ts) is listed as it is. Index files, tests and declaration files are left out. A file which sits directly in the source directory, beside the folders, is a module of its own (unless it is index or main). The first comment of a folder's index.ts (or the header comment of such a file) describes its module. The comments on your code are the documentation, and the types come from the code itself, so @module, @memberOf, @typedef and the {Type} of @param are not needed. typedoc is an optional peer dependency (like typescript), install it in your project with npm install --save-dev typedoc (this needs a typescript version it supports). - jsdoc (for a plain JavaScript project, where TypeDoc has no real types to read) - scans your source (.js, .mjs and .cjs files, leaving out tests and minified .min.js copies) recursively with jsdoc itself, rendered with a modern theme (clean-jsdoc-theme by default, used instead of jsdoc's own classic default template) instead of the manual .jsdoc.conf.js setup described further below. jsdoc and whichever theme you configure are optional peer dependencies, install them with npm install --save-dev jsdoc clean-jsdoc-theme (or your own chosen theme package). Add the following to the exports in your build-tools.config.json: While docs.enabled is on, gulp build generates the documentation instead of the readme, so your README.md stays hand-written (a short overview which links to the documentation). If you also export docs from your gulpfile you can run it on its own with gulp docs, and can then add the script "docs": "gulp docs". To make generating the documentation a deliberate step instead, set docs.inBuild to false: gulp build then generates neither the documentation nor the readme, and gulp docs is the only thing that writes to docs.to. This suits a docs.to which points into another repository (a website, say): a build on a work-in-progress branch no longer rewrites the published documentation, which you regenerate when you release instead. For example with release-it, in .release-it.json: Browser automation (optional) Unlike the rest of this file, this isn't a build-tools.config.json-driven feature with its own task - it's a pair of plain functions (partials.loadPlaywright/partials.launchBrowser and partials.serveStatic) for whatever your own script needs a real browser for: verifying a page that only works correctly in a real browser (for example one using , which no DOM-simulation library executes at all), or taking a real screenshot. playwright is an optional peer dependency, install it in your project with npm install --save-dev playwright, then fetch a real browser binary once per machine (not per project) with npx playwright install chromium - if that fails with "Playwright does not support chromium on ", your OS is too old for the current release; either upgrade it or pin an older playwright version known to still support it (confirmed: 1.62.1 is the newest release that still installs and runs real headless Chromium on Ubuntu 20.04). serveStatic exists because a page loaded directly from a file:// path resolves any root-relative asset path (/browser/...) against the filesystem root instead of the page's own directory - serving it over real HTTP avoids that entirely, and is also the right fix for the exact same problem in a jsdom-based test. Configure lint rule overrides (optional) sourceLint lints your real source directly (not the compiled dist/browser output) with neostandard. Occasionally a rule is wrong for your project specifically, rather than something to fix in your code - for example a test which deliberately contains a string of literal ${...} text (simulating another module's real source, not a mistaken non-template string), which trips neostandard's no-template-curly-in-string rule as a false positive. lint.rules layers ESLint rule overrides on top of neostandard's own rules, scoped to the same files neostandard itself lints: Empty by default, so a project that never sets this gets exactly neostandard's own rules, unchanged. Prefer fixing the actual code (or, for one specific line, an eslint-disable-next-line comment) over this when the finding is real - reach for lint.rules only when the rule itself doesn't fit your project. Configure Scripts In your package.json file, add the following scripts: Usage Run any of the above commands with gulp or npm run.

content: partials Micro-functions used as components for the main gulp functions. - Version: 3.0.0 - Author: Joshua Heagle \ --- Static Methods Resolve the installed directory of an optional peer dependency, from the project being built rather than from this package. Deliberately not requirePeer/importPeer's own require(name + '/package.json') approach - that breaks for any package whose own package.json restricts its exports map and does not expose that subpath (clean-jsdoc-theme does; confirmed live, not assumed - resolving its own package.json throws ERR PACKAGE PATH NOT EXPORTED in plain Node, and a differently-shaped MODULE NOT FOUND under Jest's own resolver, which still is not "not installed" either way). Walking Node's own real module-lookup directories (require.resolve.paths) and checking each on disk sidesteps the exports map entirely - this only ever reads whether / /package.json exists, never asks the module system to resolve a restricted subpath. Parameters - name (string) — The package name. - options (Object) - options.task (string) - options.installHint (string) - options.projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") Returns - string Throws - Error — With install instructions when the package is not installed. Print a file's lint messages, if it has any. Parameters - file (Vinyl) - result (Object) Returns - undefined Read a tsconfig.json file into real typescript.CompilerOptions values, using only TypeScript's stable, current, public config-reading API (the same one tsc --project itself uses internally) - never ts.convertCompilerOptionsFromJson, which is exactly the kind of internal/legacy surface that broke gulp-typescript when a removed API call started throwing under TypeScript 7. Parameters - configPath (string) — Path to a tsconfig.json file. Returns - ts.CompilerOptions — TypeScript's compiler options Other Appends all the jsdoc comments to the readme file. Assumes empty or templated file. Configure this with 'readmeSearch', 'readmePath', 'readmeFile', and 'readmeOptions'. jsdoc-to-markdown only recognizes .js files, even though it parses real ESM syntax just fine once it reads one - readme.fromEsm (empty by default) names .mjs files to include anyway, converted on the fly (see convertMjsFilesForDocs) and cleaned up again once this has read them, win or lose. Returns - string Uint8Array Create a chokidar instance which watches and triggers change when the globed files are modified. Returns - FSWatcher Deletes all the distribution and browser files (used before create a new build). Configure array of directories to remove with 'cleanPaths'. Returns - Promise. Copy some files to a different location. Parameters - srcPath (string array) - destPath (string) - options (Object, optional) - options.base (string, optional) — Passed through to gulp's own src(pattern, {base}), to preserve srcPath's own subdirectory structure in destPath instead of flattening it. Returns - stream.Stream Build the distribution for a given source pattern. Parameters - srcPath (string array, optional, default: "'src/config/path/dist/for'") - destPath (string, optional, default: "'dist/config/path'") Returns - stream.Stream Retrieve the correct distFor search path based on TS Config. Parameters - useTs (module:gulpConfig\ FlagStringSetting, optional, default: "'config/for/ts'") Returns - string When using TypeScript, ensure that we process the ts first then run babel (dist) Parameters - srcPath (string, optional, default: "'src/config/path/dist/for'") - distFinalPath (string, optional, default: "'dist/config/path'") - tsSearch (string, optional, default: "'ts/search/config/path'") Returns - function Load gulp-imagemin, an optional peer dependency: image optimization is off by default and its binary-download dependency chain is heavy, so it is only required once the images task actually runs, and it is resolved from the consuming project's own directory rather than from this package. Parameters - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The project directory to resolve gulp-imagemin from. Returns - function — The gulp-imagemin plugin factory. Throws - Error — With install instructions when gulp-imagemin is missing or is the ESM-only upstream release. Load the plugins gulp-imagemin exports by name (gifsicle, mozjpeg, optipng and svgo), each a promise of a plugin factory, for when they need options of their own (see images.jpegQuality). Resolved like loadImagemin. Parameters - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The project directory to resolve gulp-imagemin from. Returns - Object. — The plugin factories, by name. The plugins imagemin uses by default, with mozjpeg set to the given JPEG quality instead of its own default (75). Parameters - jpegQuality (number) — The mozjpeg quality, 0 to 100. - plugins (Object.\ , optional, default: "loadImageminPlugins()") — The plugin factories, by name. Returns - Array. — The plugins, in imagemin's default order. Move and optimize images into the browser directory. Parameters - imageSrc (string array, optional, default: "src/images/pattern") - imageDest (string, optional, default: "dest/image/folder") Returns - stream.Stream Resolve jsdoc's own CLI entry point. jsdoc has no stable programmatic Node API for generating HTML docs (unlike TypeDoc's Application.bootstrap()/convert()/generateDocs()) - gulp-jsdoc3, the established gulp wrapper, is stale, and its own README admits jsdoc does not support piped input in the first place, a real anti-pattern for this project's own gulp-stream conventions. Running its real CLI via child process is the portable way in - confirmed via npm view jsdoc bin, which reports "jsdoc.js" at the package root. Parameters - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") Returns - string Resolve a jsdoc theme package's own template directory, for jsdoc's own opts.template config key: the folder holding its publish.js. That is the package root for a classic jsdoc template (clean-jsdoc-theme 4.x included), but dist for a bundled one (clean-jsdoc-theme 5.x). Parameters - name (string) - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") Returns - string Generate the HTML documentation of a plain-JavaScript project with jsdoc, using jsdoc.base.js's own shared config (plugins, includePattern/excludePattern) as the starting point rather than a parallel one - the same base a project's own .jsdoc.conf.js has always been able to extend, just with source.include and the output options generated here instead of hand-maintained per project. Configure this with 'docs.from', 'docs.to', 'docs.index', 'docs.theme' and 'docs.title'. Parameters - srcPath (string Array.\ , optional, default: "gulpConfig.get('docs.from')") — The directory (or directories and files) holding the JS source. - outPath (string, optional, default: "gulpConfig.get('docs.to')") — The directory the documentation is generated into (cleared first). - runJsdoc (function, optional) — Runs the jsdoc CLI, tests can inject a stand-in. Returns - function — A gulp task, it accepts an optional callback and returns a promise. Lint the project's source (srcPath: .js, .mjs and .cjs, plus .ts when typescript.enabled) with neostandard and write the automatic fixes back in place. Shared by the sourceLint (build) and lint (standalone) tasks. Parameters - options (Object, optional, default: "{}") - options.failOnError (boolean, optional, default: false) — Fail once linting finishes if any errors could not be fixed. Returns - stream.Stream Import an ES module (or any module) with a real dynamic import(), whichever build (ESM or CommonJS) this runs from. Parameters - specifier (string) — The package name, or the URL of a file. Returns - Promise. — The module namespace. Load an optional peer dependency (one which is only needed once a task runs, so projects which never use that task do not have to install it) with require(), from the project being built rather than from this package. When it is missing the error explains how to install it. Parameters - name (string) — The package name. - options (Object) - options.task (string) — The task which needs the package, for the error message. - options.installHint (string) — How to install it, for the error message. - options.esmOnlyMessage (string, optional) — The error message when the package turns out to be ESM-only (it cannot be require()d). - options.projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The folder of the project (which has the package.json) being built. Returns - — Whatever the package exports. Throws - Error — With install instructions when the package is not installed. Import an optional peer dependency which ships ESM-only, from the project being built. See requirePeer. Parameters - name (string) — The package name. - options (Object) - options.task (string) — The task which needs the package, for the error message. - options.installHint (string) — How to install it, for the error message. - options.projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The folder of the project (which has the package.json) being built. Returns - Promise. — The module namespace. Throws - Error — With install instructions when the package is not installed. Find Playwright (headless-browser automation) of the project being built, an optional peer dependency only needed by whatever actually drives a real browser - projects which never do never need it installed. Parameters - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The folder of the project (which has the package.json) being built. Returns - Object — The Playwright module. Throws - Error — With install instructions when playwright is not installed. Launch a real headless Chromium browser via Playwright. See loadPlaywright. Parameters - load (function, optional, default: "loadPlaywright") — Which Playwright to launch - swappable in tests. - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The folder of the project (which has the package.json) being built. Returns - Promise. — The running Playwright browser - close it yourself (browser.close()) once done with it. Throws - Error — With install instructions when playwright is not installed. Minify files and rename the output with '.min' extension. Returns - Lint every file streaming through with neostandard and, unless fix is false, apply the automatic fixes to the file's contents so a following dest() writes the fixed version. Remaining problems are printed along with a summary once the stream ends; they only fail the stream when failOnError is set (the standalone lint task), never during build. One ESLint instance is built from the first file's own cwd and reused for the rest of the stream, since every file in a given lint pass shares the same project (and so the same config). Parameters - options (Object, optional, default: "{}") - options.fix (boolean, optional, default: true) — Apply neostandard's automatic fixes to the file contents. - options.ts (boolean, optional, default: false) — Lint .ts files too, with type-aware rules (see neostandard's ts option). - options.rules (Object.\ , optional, default: "{}") — ESLint rule overrides layered on top of neostandard's own rules (see gulp.config.mjs's lint.rules). - options.failOnError (boolean, optional, default: false) — Emit an error once the stream ends if any lint errors remain after fixing, so a command-line run exits non-zero. - loadEslint (function, optional) — Resolves an ESLint-shaped linter. Real callers should never need to pass this - it exists so tests can supply a stand-in, since this project's CommonJS-transform-based Jest setup cannot execute a real dynamic import() of neostandard (ESM-only). Returns - stream.Transform — With a totals property ({errors, warnings}), complete once the stream ends. Copy a readme template into the README.md file. Returns - Delete a directory and everything in it, resolving only once it is really gone. A single rm can leave a directory behind - most often when something is still writing into it (a build task, a watcher, a dev server) or has it briefly locked (EBUSY/EPERM/ENOTEMPTY) - which silently leaves stale output for the next build. So: Node's own retry-with-back-off handles the transient errors, then the directory is checked and removed again if it was recreated, and a clear error is raised rather than carrying on with stale output. Parameters - dirPath (string) Returns - Promise. — Resolves with dirPath once the directory no longer exists (or already didn't). Throws - Error — If the directory still exists after several attempts. Pick which engine generates the HTML documentation: docs.method picks it explicitly; left unset (false, the default), it's inferred from typescript.enabled - every existing TypeScript project's config, which never sets method, keeps producing TypeDoc output exactly as it always has. Returns - 'typedoc' 'jsdoc' Run this function when the watched files are modified. 1. Find the sub-folders within src path 1. Maintain the folders, but use distPath for base 1. Remove base folder and return dist path with correct sub-folders Parameters - path (string) Returns - stream.Stream Example Build the CSS for a given source pattern. Parameters - srcSearch (string array, optional, default: "'src/config/path/sass/for'") - cssPath (string, optional, default: "'css/config/path'") Returns - stream.Stream Serve a directory's real files over plain HTTP, for anything that needs a page loaded from a real URL rather than a bare file:// path - most commonly, a page using root-relative asset paths (/browser/...), which a file:// load resolves against the filesystem root instead of the page's own directory. Parameters - rootDir (string) — The directory to serve. - port (number, optional, default: 0) — The port to listen on; 0 picks any free port. Returns - Promise. — The running server, and its base URL - close the server yourself (server.close()) once done with it. Wrap a stream in a promise that resolves once it finishes writing. Parameters - stream (stream.Stream) Returns - Promise. Load the project's own copy of TypeScript (an optional peer dependency, only needed when the typescript task is enabled) from the project being built, so projects which do not use TypeScript never need it installed. Parameters - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The folder of the project (which has the package.json) being built. Returns - Object — The TypeScript compiler API module. Throws - Error — With install instructions when typescript is not installed. Starting at the source directory, find all the ts files and convert them into the distribution directory. Parameters - srcPath (string array, optional, default: "''") - distPath (string, optional, default: "''") - loadTsCompile (function, optional) — Resolves the gulp-ts-compile default export. Real callers should never need to pass this - it exists so tests can inject a stand-in compiler, sidestepping the genuine dynamic import() above that this project's current CommonJS-transform-based Jest setup cannot execute without a broader (and riskier) migration to Jest's native ESM support. gulp-ts-compile's own test suite already covers real TypeScript-compile correctness - this function's own tests only need to verify its config resolution and stream wiring. Returns - function Find the TypeDoc of the project being built (an optional peer dependency, only needed when the docs task is enabled) and load it, so projects which do not document TypeScript never need it installed. Parameters - projectPath (string, optional, default: "process.cwd()") — The folder of the project (which has the package.json) being built. Returns - Promise. — The TypeDoc module. Throws - Error — With install instructions when typedoc is not installed. Describe what a source file exports: whether it has a default export, and whether it has any named exports. Parameters - ts (Object) — The TypeScript compiler API. - filePath (string) Returns - Object The description of a folder for its module: the first doc comment of the folder's index file, without its tags (@module, @file, ...), or an empty string when there is none. Parameters - folderPath (string) Returns - string The description of a source file for its module: its first doc comment without the tags (@module, @file, ...), when that comment is a header (it is followed by an import or export, so it does not document a declaration itself), or an empty string. Parameters - filePath (string) Returns - string Write one entry file per folder of the source directory into the entry directory. TypeDoc makes a module of every entry file, so the modules of the documentation mirror the folders. Nested folders are modules of their own, named by their path (utilities/parsers), and a folder's module holds only the files directly in it. The default export of each source file is re-exported under the name of the file (the source files hold one function each), and anything else a file exports is re-exported as it is (that is where the types.ts files go). Index files (the barrels), tests and declaration files are left out, but the first doc comment of a folder's index file becomes the description of its module. A file which sits beside the folders (not an index, main or browser file) is a module of its own, described by its header comment. A source directory with no folders gets a single entry called index. Parameters - ts (Object) — The TypeScript compiler API. - srcDir (string) — The directory holding the TypeScript source. - entryDir (string) — The directory to write the entry files into. Returns - Array. — The paths of the entry files. Generate the HTML documentation of a TypeScript project with TypeDoc, straight from the TypeScript source, so the types (and the comments on them) are documented from where they are defined. The modules mirror the folders of the source, see writeDocEntries. Configure this with 'docs.from', 'docs.to', 'docs.index', 'docs.title', 'docs.tsconfig' and 'docs.logLevel'. Parameters - srcPath (string, optional, default: "gulpConfig.get('docs.from')") — The directory holding the TypeScript source. - outPath (string, optional, default: "gulpConfig.get('docs.to')") — The directory the documentation is generated into (cleared first). - loadDocs (function, optional) — Resolves the TypeDoc module, tests can inject a stand-in. Returns - function — A gulp task, it accepts an optional callback and returns a promise.

description: Import these functions to your own project to customize your build pipeline.
content: js-build-tools Import these functions to your own project to customize your build pipeline. - Author: Joshua Heagle \ --- Other Runs several processes to build and validate the project. Cleans and lints the source, distributes and minifies, bundles and minifies, creates the readme, then runs the tests. Returns - stream.Stream Starting at each bundle's own entry point (dist.main for the primary bundle, or its own override from browser.bundles), bundle all the reachable files into a single file per bundle and store them in the specified output directory. A project with no browser.bundles entries gets exactly the one bundle it always did; each additional entry produces its own separate bundle (for example, a render-only variant built from a different entry point than the full bundle). A bundle's name does double duty: it names the output file (name.js) and, via browserify's standalone option, is also the name its exports are exposed under - as a global when loaded with a bare tag, or as the module when required via CommonJS/AMD. Without this, a bundle built from a real entry point (one that actually exports something) builds successfully but exposes nothing a consumer can reach. Two escape hatches from browser.config.json keep an unwanted dependency (or a dependency's dependency) out of the bundle: 'ignore' replaces it with an empty object (safe when your code never actually calls into it - for example a library's default option value you always override with your own) and 'exclude' leaves it out entirely (your code must not require it, or provide it another way, such as a separate script tag). Returns - stream.Stream Creates the minified file for every bundle (the primary bundle, plus any additional ones from browser.bundles). The minify step itself never varies per bundle, so this is one shared src()/dest() pipeline (inside minifyFor) fed every bundle's filename at once, rather than one pipeline per bundle - gulp's src() accepts an array of paths natively. Returns - Generate the README.md file based off of the template, then append the generated documentation. Returns - stream.Stream Copy files from one place to another - any number of { from, to, base? } entries, configured via copyFiles. A project with no copyFiles entries gets a task that does nothing. Meant to be run explicitly (its own script, e.g. gulp copyFiles), not folded into the default build - a bundle (or any other file this copies) is often the live, publicly-reachable version of something, so publishing it elsewhere should be a deliberate step, not a side effect of every routine local build. Reuses copyFor (already shared with copyFonts) rather than a fresh src()/dest() pair - that keeps its existing encoding: false fix (Gulp 5's default utf8 handling corrupts binary files such as fonts or a minified bundle) instead of silently losing it in a parallel implementation. Each entry runs as its own independent copyFor(), awaited via Promise.all rather than merged into one combined stream (mergeStream, the pattern bundle.mjs uses) - that pattern assumes every merged stream ends up at the same shared destination; here, each entry can have a genuinely different one, and merging streams that each already terminate at their own separate dest() hit a real "write after end" error in practice. Returns - Promise. Move the font files into the browser directory. Returns - stream.Stream Recommended as the default task, runs the simple dist and bundle tasks. Parameters - done (function, optional, default: null) Returns - stream.Stream Simplified distribution tasks which will use arguments from distFor. Returns - Creates minified versions of the dist files. Returns - Generate the HTML documentation with whichever engine docs.method (or its typescript.enabled-based default) resolves to - see module:partials.resolveDocsMethod. The standalone counterpart to build's own internal branching, for running gulp docs directly instead of as part of a full build. Parameters - done (function, optional) Returns - Move and optimize the images into the browser folder using configured settings. Returns - stream.Stream Generate the HTML documentation of a plain-JavaScript project from its source, with a modern jsdoc theme instead of jsdoc's own classic default. Turn it on with docs.enabled and docs.method: 'jsdoc' (the default when typescript.enabled is off), see module:partials.jsdocDocsFor. Returns - function The standalone lint command (gulp lint, or npm run lint): the same linting and fixing as sourceLint, but it fails (exits non-zero) when any errors remain that neostandard could not fix automatically. Returns - Micro-functions used as components for the main gulp functions. - Version: 3.0.0 - Author: Joshua Heagle \ Applies neostandard linting (js-build-tools' chosen style) to the real, hand-written source - not the compiled dist/browser output, which is generated and so was never going to pass a hand-authored-code style check (every compiler/bundler emits its own boilerplate - import aliasing, interop headers - that only looks like a style violation). Includes test files: there is no reason to hold tests to a lower style bar than the rest of the source. When typescript.enabled, the real TypeScript source is linted too, with type-aware rules. Runs as part of build, where remaining errors are reported but never fail it. Returns - Run all tests with jest. Configure where tests are located by using 'testPath'. Returns - Promise.
